t: Count Pairs of Equal Substrings With Minimum Difference — Only Single Characters Can Win
o:
## Understanding the problem

Choose a substring firstString[i..j] and a substring secondString[a..b] with identical content; the quadruple costs j − a. Among all content-equal pairs we must count how many attain the global minimum cost. A shrinking argument settles everything: if a matching pair has length ≥ 2, trim BOTH substrings to their first characters — equality survives, a is unchanged, j decreases — so the cost strictly drops. Minimizers therefore use single characters: pairs (firstString[i], secondString[a]) with equal letters minimizing i − a.

For a fixed letter c, the cost i − a shrinks when i is its FIRST occurrence in firstString and a is its LAST occurrence in secondString; every other placement is dominated. Hence each common letter contributes at most one optimal quadruple, and the answer equals the number of letters tied at the smallest i − a.

**Example walkthrough:** "abcd" vs "bccda": letter a gives 0 − 4 = −4, b gives 1 − 0 = 1, c gives 2 − 2 = 0, d gives 3 − 3 = 0. The minimum −4 belongs to letter a alone → answer 1. When the alphabets do not intersect (example 2) no quadruple exists → answer 0. Lengths up to 2·10⁵ forbid comparing all index pairs, hinting that only per-letter extremes matter.
k: Trimming equal substrings down to their first characters preserves equality, keeps a fixed, and lowers j — longer substrings can never achieve the minimum.
Per letter, pairing its first occurrence in firstString with its last occurrence in secondString minimizes j − a; all other index choices are dominated.
Only 26 letters exist: two linear scans build first/last tables and a 26-way comparison finishes in O(n + m).

a.n: Approach 1: Scan all equal character pairs
a.i: Ignore substring lengths entirely — they are dominated — and evaluate every index pair (i, a) with matching letters, maintaining the smallest difference seen and how many pairs tie it. At lengths of 2·10⁵ this performs up to 4·10¹⁰ comparisons, purely conceptual, but it defines the ground truth the optimized solution must reproduce, including tie counting.
s: Double loop over i in firstString and a in secondString.
When the characters match, compute diff = i − a.
diff < best resets best and count; diff == best increments count.
a.t: O(n · m) — every index pair inspected; ~4·10¹⁰ operations at maximum lengths (TLE)

a.n: Approach 2: First/last occurrence tables per letter
a.i: Collapse the double loop using the domination argument: record each letter’s first index in firstString and last index in secondString during two passes, then compare at most 26 candidates firstPos[c] − lastPos[c]. The minimum is the global minimum and its tie count is the answer — provably identical to the brute force because within a letter only the (first, last) combination can tie the optimum.
s: Build firstPos[c] = earliest index of c in firstString (keep the first hit) and lastPos[c] = latest index of c in secondString (keep overwriting).
For each letter c present in both strings, compute diff = firstPos[c] − lastPos[c].
Apply the same update rule: strict improvement resets count, ties increment it.
a.t: O(n + m + 26) — two string passes plus a constant-size alphabet scan

w:
## Wrap-up

State the shrinking lemma first — it IS the problem. Then the per-letter domination argument collapses O(n·m) into O(n+m). Explaining why tie-counting stays consistent (exactly one dominating combination per tying letter) shows real command of the solution.

**Common pitfalls**

- Reaching for multi-character machinery (rolling hashes, suffix automata) — unnecessary once the lemma is on the table.
- Tracking the LAST occurrence in firstString or the FIRST in secondString; both inflate j − a and break tie counts.
- Letters missing from either string need sentinel handling (-1 / absence checks) before differencing indices.
- Negative differences are perfectly legal (the letter appears late in secondString); initialize best to +infinity, never clamp at 0.

**Likely follow-ups:** report the actual quadruples; extend to k strings; or swap the alphabet for Unicode (hash maps replace the 26-slot arrays).
